input.question: when you're sick, why do symptoms seem worse at night / when trying to sleep?
input.ground_truth: One of the mechanisms at work is the cortisol level. Cortisol is a steroid hormone your body produces, that (among very many other things) suppresses your immune system. But the Cortisol levels vary during the course of a day. As you might have guessed, the concentration of cortisol in your blood decreases during the day and reaches lower levels in the late evening and night. So basically your symptoms get worse, because there is less immunosuppressive Cortisol to fight the inflammation, which leads to more swelling and stronger pain signals being sent.

Question: when you're sick, why do symptoms seem worse at night / when trying to sleep?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine your body is like a house, and when you’re sick, there are little germs trying to make trouble inside your house.

At night, your house (your body) gets quiet and still because you’re resting and not moving around as much. When the house is quiet, you can hear small sounds more clearly—like a creaky floor or a dripping faucet.

When you’re trying to sleep, your body is also trying to fix itself. It sends out special helpers (like white blood cells) to fight the germs. These helpers can make you feel achy, sniffly, or have a sore throat, just like how a cleaning crew might make a little mess while cleaning your house.

Also, at night, your body’s temperature can go down a little, and sometimes germs like to be more active when it’s cooler. That can make you feel worse too.

So, at night, you notice the sickness more because your body is working hard to get better, and everything is quiet so you notice those yucky feelings more!
